text: Given a circular integer array nums, return the largest possible sum of a non-empty subarray. The end wraps around to the start, but each element can be used at most once.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — a subarray is still contiguous, but now it can go past the last index and keep going from index zero. It can't be empty, and it can't use the same index twice. So the longest one is the whole array, once. And I only return the sum. Is that right?
Yes. Non-empty, at most once per element, and just the sum.

Okay. Then every answer is one of two shapes. Either it's a normal subarray in the middle, like the classic straight-line maximum subarray. Or it wraps: it takes a piece from the end and a piece from the start. And here's the trick. If a subarray wraps, then what it leaves out is one normal block in the middle. So the wrap sum is the total minus that middle block. I'll keep that in mind. Are there any constraints on the input size?
The array has up to three times ten to the fourth elements, and each value is between minus thirty thousand and plus thirty thousand.

Got it. So I want one pass. The biggest sum in size is thirty thousand times thirty thousand, which is nine hundred million. That's about forty-two percent of the int limit, so a plain int is enough. Let me run through the example: five, minus three, five. The normal best is the whole array — five minus three plus five is seven. But if I wrap, I can take the last five and then the first five, and skip the minus three. That's ten. So the answer is ten. And look: ten is the total, seven, minus the block I skipped, minus three. The other two examples: one, minus two, three, minus two gives three — just the three alone. And minus three, minus two, minus three gives minus two, the single biggest number.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would be to try every start index, then walk forward up to n steps with the index wrapping modulo n, and keep a running sum. That's quadratic time. It's correct, and I'd keep it as a brute force to test against. But at thirty thousand elements it's too slow. This problem reminds me of Kadane's algorithm — the running extend-or-restart scan that solves maximum subarray on a straight line, and it fits here because the non-wrapping case is exactly that. Kadane already gives me the best normal subarray. For the wrap case, I flip the question. I don't search for the best wrap. I search for the worst normal block — the minimum subarray — and cut it out. Total minus the minimum block is the best wrap. And I can find the minimum block with the same Kadane, just with min instead of max. Both run in the same loop.

Here's the plan. I keep five numbers: the total of the whole circle, then a current and a best value for each Kadane. Cur-max and sub-max track the best sum ending at the current element and the best block seen so far. Cur-min and sub-min do the same for the worst block, with min swapped in for max. For each element, I add it to the total; cur-max either extends the previous run or restarts at this element, whichever is bigger; cur-min does the same, whichever is smaller; and the two records get refreshed. After the loop, if sub-max is below zero, I return sub-max. Otherwise I return the larger of sub-max and total minus sub-min — normal versus wrap. One thing worth flagging — that guard. Let me walk through it. Take minus three, minus two, minus three. The minimum block is the whole array, minus eight, which is also the total. So total minus sub-min is zero. But that zero means cut out everything, which is the empty subarray. That's not allowed. Without the guard I'd return zero, but the answer is minus two. And sub-max below zero happens exactly when every number is negative. In that case no wrap can help, so I just return sub-max. One more thing worth flagging — the guard has to check sub-max, not the total. A natural wrong idea is: if the total is negative, skip the wrap. Take one, minus three, one. The total is minus one, but the wrap — the last one plus the first one — gives two. That rule returns one. So the question is not, is the total negative. It's, is every number negative. There's a trade-off here. Another way is to double the array and run a sliding window with a monotonic deque on prefix sums. That also works in linear time, but it needs linear extra space and much more code. The min-block trick is constant space and one loop. So I'll go with that. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up — and I'll talk through it rather than read it line by line. I set up total, cur-max and cur-min at zero, sub-max at the smallest possible int, and sub-min at the largest. Then one loop over the numbers. Each element goes into the total. Cur-max becomes the larger of extending the previous run or restarting fresh at this element; cur-min is the mirror image with min. Then sub-max and sub-min each take the new record if there is one. After the loop, if sub-max is below zero the whole array is negative, so I return sub-max. Otherwise I return the larger of total minus sub-min and sub-max. That matches the plan line by line. One thing worth flagging — the start values. Sub-max starts at the smallest int and sub-min at the largest, not at zero. If sub-max started at zero, then an array holding just minus one would return zero instead of minus one. Same thing if I swap the order and update the records before the current values: the first compare would see the initial zero, which is the empty subarray. Starting cur-max at zero is fine, though, because on the first number, extend and restart are both just that number. Also, the last line still needs the max with sub-max. If I only returned total minus sub-min, then a single one would give zero, because the min block is the whole array again. The max rescues that.

Let's dry-run the code with an example. I'll use two, minus three, four, minus six, one, five, because here the wrap wins. The expected output is nine. The first element, two, starts everything at two. The minus three pulls the total to minus one; cur-max extends to minus one, but cur-min restarts at minus three — a new worst block. The four makes cur-max restart at four, a new best. Now the key row, index three, the minus six. For cur-min, extending gives one minus six, which is minus five, but minus six alone is smaller, so it restarts. The worst block becomes just index three, sum minus six, and it never gets worse after that. On the max side, cur-max restarts at index four and climbs to six at index five, so the best normal subarray is the one and the five at the end. At the end, the total is three. Sub-max is six, which is not negative, so no guard. Cut out the minus six block and I get three minus minus six, which is nine. That's every index except three — going four, five, zero, one, two around the circle. Nine beats six, so the answer is nine. That matches. Let's also test with corner cases. Five, minus three, five gives ten: total seven, min block minus three, and seven minus minus three is ten. One, minus two, three, minus two gives three: the wrap gives two, but the normal three wins. All negative — minus three, minus two, minus three — the min block equals the total, so the wrap formula gives the empty zero, and the guard returns minus two instead. Three, minus one, two, minus one is a tie: normal and wrap both give four. A single one returns one, and a single minus one returns minus one — the guard handles the negative one. And at full size: thirty thousand copies of thirty thousand give nine hundred million; all negative gives minus thirty thousand by the guard; and all thirty thousands with one minus thirty thousand in the middle gives eight hundred ninety-nine million, nine hundred seventy thousand — the wrap wins. All of it fits in an int.

Let me think about complexity here. The time complexity is linear: one pass, and the two Kadanes share the same loop. The space complexity is constant — just five integers. In the worst case it's still exactly n steps; there's no early exit and no extra work. At thirty thousand elements it takes about forty microseconds per call, and the biggest value I ever hold is nine hundred million, so there's no overflow. Oh, one more thing — I'd test this against the quadratic brute force on lots of arrays. I ran about two hundred forty thousand cases, small and large, with zero mismatches. That check matters here. The wrong guard on the total passes all three official examples, but it fails on one, minus three, one. And forgetting the guard only breaks on all-negative arrays. Bugs like that hide from a few hand-picked tests, so a brute-force check is worth it.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You reframed the wrap case as the whole circle minus one middle block, so the best wrap is the total minus the minimum subarray, and you got both with one loop. You explained why the guard is needed: on an all-negative array the min block is the whole array, so total minus sub-min is zero — the empty subarray. And you showed the guard must check sub-max, not the total, with one, minus three, one. Good work.
